patient.chief_complaint: Sudden loss of consciousness with brief shaking movements, witnessed by husband
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Patricia Holloway is a 60-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder on citalopram, hypertension, hypothyroidism, and recent community-acquired pneumonia who presents to the emergency department after a sudden loss of consciousness at home approximately 45 minutes ago. Her husband witnessed the entire event. He reports that she was standing in the kitchen, appeared to briefly sway, then suddenly became unresponsive and fell to the floor, striking the back of her head. He states she immediately exhibited rapid, irregular shaking movements of her limbs — lasting approximately 15 to 20 seconds — which he likens to 'a seizure he once saw on television.' She did not make any sound prior to collapsing and there was no warning cry. During the event, she appeared gray and he could not palpate a pulse at the carotid for approximately 8 to 10 seconds. She then abruptly resumed spontaneous movement, gasped, and within 30 seconds was awake and asking what happened. She had no post-event confusion and did not bite her tongue. She denied urinary incontinence. The husband called 911 and EMS arrived within 6 minutes, at which point the patient was fully alert and conversational, describing only mild dizziness and 'feeling strange.' She has no prior history of seizures, no prior syncopal episodes, and no family history of sudden cardiac death or seizure disorder. She notes that she has been taking all her medications as prescribed. Approximately 5 days ago she started azithromycin for a pneumonia diagnosed by her primary care physician. Two to three days ago she also began taking ondansetron for nausea, which had been prescribed to her alongside the antibiotic. She has been on citalopram 40 mg daily for four years and hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. She denies recent changes in her other medications, illicit drug use, or ingestion of herbal supplements. On further questioning she acknowledges that she had been eating poorly due to the illness and had experienced loose stools for two days prior to presentation, raising concern for possible electrolyte losses.

output.impression: 24-hour inpatient telemetry demonstrates sinus rhythm with markedly prolonged QTc (peak 545 ms) and two captured episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with torsades de pointes morphology, each self-terminating within 14 seconds. Both episodes were pause-dependent. The second episode correlated with observed brief limb movements during sleep. QTc showed progressive shortening to 480 ms at 18 hours of monitoring. No degeneration to VF. No AV block or significant pauses between episodes.

output.proposed: Citalopram 40 mg daily + azithromycin 250 mg daily + ondansetron 4 mg every 8 hours + hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily
interactions: Citalopram + azithromycin [CONTRAINDICATED]: Both prolong cardiac repolarization via hERG/IKr channel blockade. Combination produces additive QTc prolongation; torsades de pointes risk is substantially increased, particularly at citalopram doses ≥40 mg.

Citalopram + ondansetron [CONTRAINDICATED]: Ondansetron prolongs QTc via hERG channel blockade; co-administration with citalopram produces additive QTc prolongation. Combination is formally contraindicated per manufacturer labeling; markedly increased torsades de pointes risk.
Azithromycin + ondansetron [MAJOR]: Both independently prolong QTc via hERG blockade; the triple combination with citalopram compounds the additive repolarization delay further.

Hydrochlorothiazide — electrolyte interaction [MAJOR]: Thiazide diuretics cause renal potassium and magnesium wasting; hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia reduce the threshold for drug-induced QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, potentiating the cardiac toxicity of the concurrent QT-prolonging drug combination.
contraindications: Citalopram dose ≥40 mg is associated with dose-dependent QTc prolongation; concurrent use with other QT-prolonging agents (azithromycin, ondansetron, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones) is contraindicated or requires QTc monitoring and dose reduction.
Ondansetron is contraindicated in combination with other QT-prolonging drugs including SSRIs at high doses and macrolide antibiotics per current prescribing information.
Triple QT-prolonging combination (citalopram + azithromycin + ondansetron) together with thiazide-induced electrolyte depletion represents a high-risk additive QT prolongation scenario.
warnings: Hypokalemia (K+ <3.5 mEq/L) and hypomagnesemia (Mg <1.7 mg/dL) independently prolong cardiac repolarization and substantially increase the risk of drug-induced torsades de pointes — correction of electrolytes is essential when managing drug-induced QT prolongation.
Women have a longer baseline QTc than men, which confers greater susceptibility to drug-induced QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

Patients on thiazide diuretics who develop gastrointestinal illness with poor oral intake are at increased risk for electrolyte depletion, creating a vulnerability window for drug-induced long QT syndrome.
QTc should be monitored when combining any two or more QT-prolonging agents; if QTc exceeds 500 ms or increases ≥60 ms from baseline, all offending agents should be discontinued.
alternatives: For nausea management in a patient requiring an antibiotic: metoclopramide or domperidone (verify local availability); if nausea is intractable, consider a non-QT-prolonging alternative after cardiologist guidance.

For antibiotic therapy in penicillin-allergic patients: doxycycline or respiratory fluoroquinolones may be considered, but fluoroquinolones also prolong QTc — avoid in this setting until QT is normalized. Azithromycin should be discontinued.

For depression management: after QTc normalizes, citalopram dose reduction below 40 mg should be discussed with the prescribing psychiatrist; alternative SSRIs with lower QT-prolongation risk (sertraline, fluoxetine) may be considered.

results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope
results.authors: Brignole M, Moya A, de Lange FJ, et al.
results.finding: Cardiac syncope due to arrhythmia requires ECG as the first-line test. Drug-induced QT prolongation is an identifiable and reversible cause of torsades de pointes; medication review is mandatory in any syncope evaluation. Check_drug_interactions and electrolyte assessment are integral components of the syncope work-up when QT prolongation is identified on ECG.

results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope
results.authors: Shen WK, Sheldon RS, Benditt DG, et al.
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.finding: QT-prolonging medications should be identified and discontinued in any patient presenting with syncope and a prolonged QTc on ECG. Drug-induced long QT syndrome is the leading cause of acquired long QT and is both preventable and reversible through drug discontinuation and electrolyte correction.

results.title: Management of drug-induced long QT syndrome
results.authors: Drew BJ, Ackerman MJ, Funk M, et al.
results.finding: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first-line pharmacological treatment for torsades de pointes regardless of serum magnesium level. Potassium should be repleted to 4.0-4.5 mEq/L. All QT-prolonging drugs should be discontinued. Temporary pacing or isoproterenol can be used for pause-dependent torsades unresponsive to magnesium.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Cardiac syncope due to drug-induced long QT syndrome with torsades de pointes

differential.key_features: No prior unexplained syncope, no family history of sudden cardiac death or arrhythmia, and the QTc normalizes progressively after drug discontinuation — pointing to acquired rather than congenital etiology; however, an unmasked congenital substrate cannot be fully excluded until QTc normalizes off all culprit drugs.

Brief shaking movements (~15-20 s), no tongue bite, no urinary incontinence, and rapid full recovery within 30 s are characteristic of convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion during arrhythmia; EEG is normal; the torsades episodes on telemetry correlate directly with witnessed limb shaking.

differential.key_features: Polymorphic VT is present but pause-dependent onset and clear QT-prolonging drug combination identify a reversible acquired etiology rather than idiopathic VF or CPVT.
No prodrome of nausea, diaphoresis, or visual graying; no identifiable vasovagal trigger; structurally normal heart does not explain prolonged QTc; telemetry shows polymorphic VT, not bradycardia.

useless_tools.rationale: Brain MRI is not indicated for typical cardiac syncope with an identified arrhythmic substrate (drug-induced long QT / torsades); routine neuroimaging in cardiac syncope has no diagnostic yield and is not recommended by ESC or ACC/AHA syncope guidelines.
No meningismus, no fever, no encephalopathy — CSF analysis has no role in the evaluation of drug-induced cardiac syncope.
Tilt-table testing is irrelevant when a definitive arrhythmic substrate (torsades de pointes on documented telemetry) has been identified; it would not alter management.

sequence_constraints.reason: ECG identification of markedly prolonged QTc is the pivotal finding that drives admission, telemetry, and cardiology involvement; ECG must be obtained before disposition decisions.
Troponin must be assessed to exclude ACS and electrolytes must be assessed to characterise the torsades risk before finalising monitoring strategy.

critical_actions: Immediately discontinue all QT-prolonging agents (azithromycin, ondansetron, and citalopram) — remove the causative drugs
Administer IV magnesium sulfate as first-line pharmacotherapy for torsades de pointes, regardless of serum magnesium level
Replete potassium to 4.0-4.5 mEq/L IV — hypokalemia lowers the torsades threshold and must be corrected urgently
Place patient on continuous inpatient telemetry with defibrillator immediately available until QTc normalizes (<500 ms and trending down) and no further torsades episodes occur
Recognize that the witnessed brief convulsive shaking is convulsive syncope from torsades-induced cerebral hypoperfusion — NOT a primary epileptic seizure — and do not start antiepileptic drugs
Document the complete QT-prolonging drug combination in the medical record and update the patient allergy/alert profile to prevent recurrence
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue azithromycin, ondansetron, or citalopram — all three are QT-prolonging and constitute the causative drug combination; continuing any of them perpetuates the arrhythmic risk
Do not add any additional QT-prolonging agent (fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, other macrolides, methadone, haloperidol, amiodarone) while the QTc remains prolonged

Do not misdiagnose as primary epileptic seizure and start an antiepileptic drug — the convulsive movements are syncope-related, the EEG is normal, and antiepileptics do not address the QT-prolonging drug substrate
Do not discharge home while the QTc remains markedly prolonged or before a definitive downward QTc trend is documented on telemetry
Do not perform lumbar puncture — no clinical indication
key_reasoning_points: Acquired (drug-induced) long QT syndrome is caused by hERG/IKr channel blockade, which delays ventricular repolarization and creates a substrate for early afterdepolarizations triggering torsades de pointes; multiple QT-prolonging drugs have an additive effect on QTc prolongation

The triple QT-drug combination in this case (citalopram 40 mg + azithromycin + ondansetron) is a recognized high-risk polypharmacy scenario; each drug prolongs QTc independently, and their combination substantially elevates torsades risk above that of any single agent

Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia — caused here by thiazide diuresis and poor oral intake during illness — independently prolong cardiac repolarization and markedly potentiate drug-induced QT prolongation, lowering the torsades threshold

Women have a longer baseline QTc than men (pharmacogenomic difference in IKr current density), conferring approximately twofold higher susceptibility to drug-induced long QT and torsades de pointes at equivalent drug exposures

The witnessed 15-20 seconds of limb shaking with rapid recovery, no tongue bite, no post-ictal confusion, and negative EEG are characteristic of convulsive syncope from transient cerebral hypoperfusion during torsades — not an epileptic seizure; the telemetry records the arrhythmic cause directly

Torsades de pointes is typically pause-dependent: the characteristic short-long-short RR sequence preceding each episode (visible on telemetry) is a hallmark distinguishing it from other forms of polymorphic VT

red_herrings.data_point: Witnessed rapid, irregular shaking movements of the limbs lasting 15-20 seconds, husband states it 'looked like a seizure'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors clinician toward primary epilepsy work-up (EEG, neurology referral, antiepileptic drug initiation) and away from the ECG-driven cardiac diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The shaking represents convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion during self-terminating torsades de pointes; confirmed by normal EEG and two captured torsades episodes on telemetry coinciding with witnessed limb movements

red_herrings.data_point: Triple QT-prolonging drug combination (citalopram + azithromycin + ondansetron) all present in patient.medications
red_herrings.intended_effect: A clinician not specifically reviewing the medication list for QT-prolonging drug interactions — or one who considers each drug individually rather than their combined effect — may fail to identify the causative polypharmacy and attribute the prolonged QTc to a single agent or to a congenital cause
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The drug combination is the primary driver of acquired long QT; check_drug_interactions is required to flag the triple interaction and the additive electrolyte contribution of hydrochlorothiazide

clinical_pearls: Acquired (drug-induced) long QT syndrome is the most common cause of QTc prolongation encountered in clinical practice; polypharmacy with multiple QT-prolonging agents carries additive risk that is often underappreciated when each drug is evaluated in isolation

The triple combination of a high-dose SSRI (citalopram ≥40 mg), a macrolide antibiotic (azithromycin), and a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron) is a recognized high-risk QT-prolonging combination — each pair has a known interaction, and the triple combination is particularly hazardous

Women have a longer baseline QTc than men due to sex-based differences in IKr (cardiac repolarizing potassium current) and are approximately twofold more susceptible to drug-induced torsades de pointes at equivalent drug concentrations

Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia are critical potentiating factors for drug-induced long QT; thiazide diuretics are a common cause of both electrolyte deficiencies, and illness-related poor oral intake can compound the deficit

Torsades de pointes is characteristically pause-dependent (short-long-short RR triggering) and self-terminating in most cases, but can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation; IV magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment regardless of serum magnesium level

Convulsive syncope (brief, irregular limb movements from cerebral hypoperfusion during any syncopal episode) is frequently misinterpreted as epileptic seizure; the distinction is critical to avoid inappropriate antiepileptic drug therapy
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools; 2 grounded red herrings (convulsive presentation anchoring toward seizure; polypharmacy QT interaction requiring drug-list synthesis); requires integration of ECG QTc + electrolytes + drug interaction check to identify the reversible cause; check_drug_interactions and cardiac monitoring both load-bearing; EEG optional for seizure exclusion.
